question: I'm applying from India for a German student visa. Do I need an APS certificate?
answer: Generally yes: for a German national student visa from India, an APS certificate is always mandatory unless an exception applies [S2]. You do not need one if: you will obtain a non-German degree in Germany; you plan PhD/postdoc studies; you have a scholarship from German or EU public funds; or your studies build on a non-Indian school certificate (e.g. International Baccalaureate) or a non-Indian degree [S2]. Universities may also require it for admission: TUM says applicants with an Indian school or university degree must have their certificates checked by APS in New Delhi and attend an interview [S5]. Note that where you apply depends on your case: German bachelor/master students needing APS, scholarship holders and PhD/postdoc applicants go to VFS, while non-German-degree students apply at the Embassy or a Consulate [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with the German mission in India.

question: What kind of account do most international students use to prove they can pay for their studies in Germany?
answer: Most international students use a blocked account, called a 'Sperrkonto', as proof of sufficient funds, with the money shown as a credit to the account [S1]. A Sperrkonto must meet certain requirements: it may only allow a limited amount of withdrawals each month, and you can only close it with approval from an embassy, consulate or the competent foreigners authority [S1]. The German embassy in India currently asks for €11,904 for your first year, with no more than €992 withdrawable per month [S4]. If you prefer not to use a Sperrkonto, alternatives include a formal obligation letter from a sponsor in Germany or proof of a recognised scholarship [S1][S4]. Sperrkonten are available from a range of providers, and the best approach is to get advice from the German embassy or consulate [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm current requirements with the responsible authority.

question: If I finish a degree in Germany but need time to find a job, how long can I stay on the post-study permit?
answer: You can stay up to 18 months after graduating to look for a job that matches your qualifications [S2][S5]. This option is only available immediately after graduation, so it is lost if you first go abroad for a job [S1]. Key conditions: you must prove you can cover your living expenses and have health insurance [S2][S3]. During these 18 months you may work without restriction, including internships, self-employment or freelancing [S3][S5]. If you find a suitable job, you can get a residence permit for employment [S2]. Stays outside Germany longer than six months automatically end the permit unless the Foreigners Registration Department has agreed in writing beforehand [S3]. If you start a new degree and don't finish it, you lose any remaining months [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with your local Foreigners Registration Department.

question: While I'm on the 18-month job-search permit after graduating in Germany, am I allowed to work?
answer: Yes. During the up-to-18-month job-search period after graduating, you are allowed to work without restriction [S2][S3]. You can take any job, not just one related to your degree, including internships or trainee posts, and you may also work self-employed or as a freelancer [S2][S4]. Key conditions: you must keep proving that you can cover your living expenses yourself and, per the DAAD guide, that you have health insurance [S2][S4]. If you find a job appropriate to your qualifications during these 18 months, you can then get a residence permit for employment [S2]. Note that the permit cannot be extended beyond 18 months for further job search [S5]. Also, a stay abroad (e.g. an internship) of more than six months automatically ends the permit unless agreed in writing beforehand with the Foreigners Registration Department [S4]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with your local foreigners' authority.

question: In Germany, should I usually book a specialist directly, or start with a general doctor?
answer: Usually, start with a general practitioner (GP, called Hausarzt). In most cases the GP is your first point of contact; they assess whether you need a specialist and refer you if required [S3][S1]. If not, they may simply prescribe medicine, which you pick up at a pharmacy [S3]. Exceptions: if you already know you need a specialist (e.g., a dermatologist), you can contact them directly [S1], and for toothache or dental check-ups you can book a dental practice yourself [S2]. Whether you can book a specialist yourself can depend on the medical field, and specialist appointments can take time [S2]. Practical tips: make an appointment by phone or in person, since waiting times can be long, and bring your insurance card [S4]. GPs work only on weekdays; at weekends use an on-call clinic or call 116 117 [S5]. Check with your health insurer for your specific case.

question: Can a student residence permit in Munich cover a required preparatory language course before a full-time degree?
answer: Yes. In Munich, a residence permit for the purpose of studying also covers preparatory measures such as a preparatory language course, a preparatory college or a compulsory work placement [S1]. The key condition is that you already have a guaranteed place on a full-time degree programme at the relevant educational institution [S1]. If your admission is only conditional, or in other preparatory cases, granting the permit is at the discretion of the Service Centre for Immigration and Naturalisation [S1]. Berlin's guidance similarly counts a preparatory language course as a preparatory measure where admission to your course of study is tied to attending it [S3]. If you don't have a guaranteed place, Munich has a separate study-preparation permit; for a preparatory language course it is limited to a maximum of 18 months [S2]. This is not legal advice; please confirm your case with the Munich Service Centre for Immigration and Naturalisation.

question: What should I do at Sabancı after submitting my Turkish residence permit file, and who decides the outcome?
answer:
After you submit your file to the IRO, it is delivered to the Istanbul Provincial Immigration Administration, and you receive the result within 30-90 days by email/SMS and on the e-ikamet website [S1]. The IRO does not receive results, so you should check the website regularly [S1]. Card preparation can take up to 90 days, and the card is sent to the address on the address document you submitted; tracking it is your own responsibility [S1]. If you gave the Tuzla Campus as your address, the Communication Center will receive the card and notify you [S1]. Once you have the card, send a copy to irolegal@sabanciuniv.edu and studentinfo@sabanciuniv.edu [S1]. It is also not recommended to leave Türkiye before you get the card, because this may lead to rejection [S5].

The Directorate General of Migration Management evaluates and decides your application, not the university [S1][S5]. This is general guidance, not legal advice; please confirm with the authorities.

question: How soon after getting a residence permit card should I register my address at Sabancı?
answer:
You must register your address within 20 days of receiving your residence permit card, and again whenever your address changes [S1]. Erasmus and Exchange students can skip this if they will not extend their permits in Turkey [S1].

Key conditions and steps:
- Book an appointment through the Immigration Office Appointment System (you need e-Devlet access) and attend in person on the appointment day [S1].
- You must be over 18, your card must be active, and you must be in İstanbul [S2].
- If you live in the university dormitories or in Tuzla, Pendik, Kartal, Maltepe, Şile, Adalar or Kadıköy, you register at the Pendik District Immigration Office [S2].
- Afterwards, you can get a residence certificate (Yerleşim Yeri Belgesi) from e-Devlet, which you need for permit extensions [S2].

This is not legal advice; please confirm details with the IRO or the Immigration Office.

question: If I want to use Turkish GSS as an international student, how long after university registration do I have to apply?
answer: You must apply for General Health Insurance (GSS) within three months following your university registration [S1][S2]. Sabancı University specifies this means your first registration to the university, and that you also need your foreign national ID number before applying; you apply to the Social Security City Directorate or the Social Security Center (SGM) of the district where you live [S4]. Don't miss this deadline: if you don't apply within the 3-month period, you cannot benefit from GSS later [S3][S4]. One exception noted by Sabancı: if you change your program or program level (e.g. undergraduate to master's), you have the right to apply again [S3]. These procedures are run by state bodies and are open to change [S3], so please confirm the current rules with the Social Security Institution or your university's international office; this is not legal advice.

question: Are private health insurance policies in Türkiye accepted at every hospital?
answer:
No. Private health insurance policies in Türkiye are not valid at every hospital. Their coverage is limited, and they only work in hospitals where the insurance company has a contract [S1][S3]. For a policy to be usable at a given hospital, the insurer must have an agreement with that hospital [S2]. Even at contracted hospitals, private insurers cover services only within the limits set in your policy [S4]. Expensive private hospitals can use up those limits quickly [S2].

Practical tips:
- Check which hospitals your insurer has contracts with before you need treatment [S1][S2].
- Get an English copy of your policy and read it carefully [S4].

If you want wider access, General Health Insurance (GSS) gives you free treatment in all state hospitals [S1][S4]. You must apply for it within three months after your university registration [S1].

Rules can change, so confirm the details with your insurer or university before relying on this.

question: What kinds of housing can an international student look at in Türkiye?
answer: You have four main housing options in Türkiye: university dormitories on campus, state dormitories run by KYK (Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution) in various parts of the city, private dormitories, or an apartment you rent in the city [S2]. Private dormitories are found around most campuses and usually offer better facilities than state dormitories, but they cost more [S1]. Renting is also common: many students share a house with a few friends near their university, and prices vary by city, location and the features of the home [S1]. Homes are usually apartments with a large living room and 2 to 4 bedrooms, often with a balcony, a separate kitchen, and central or combi-boiler heating [S1]. Check current availability and costs with your university or the provider before you decide.

question: Does a Turkish student residence permit itself give me permission to take a paid job?
answer:
No. Your student residence permit does not by itself let you take a paid job in Türkiye; you need an official work permit [S1][S3]. You cannot apply for it yourself: you first find a job, and the hiring company applies for the work permit for you [S1]. Applications go to the Ministry of Labour and Social Security [S3].

Key conditions:
- Associate/undergraduate students can work only after completing their first year [S1][S3][S5], only part-time [S1], with a maximum of 24 hours per week [S5].
- Graduate students can get a work permit from their first year, for full- or part-time jobs [S1].
- In both cases, the permit is only for jobs outside the university/campus [S1].

Working without a permit is risky: your residence permit could be cancelled by the Migration Office [S4].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm with the Presidency of Migration Management or the Ministry of Labour before you take a job.

question: If I apply for Turkish GSS after the three-month deadline, can I assume I will still be covered retroactively?
answer:
No, you should not assume that. The sources say that if you miss the three-month window, you lose the right to GSS altogether. They do not mention any late or retroactive coverage. Students who do not apply within the 3-month legal period cannot benefit from this right later, and you will not have the chance to apply again [S1][S3]. Even after a timely application, you can use health care services only after the first 30 days of activation [S5].

The sources differ on when the three months start. Most count from your university registration [S2][S3]. METU counts from the first day of Fall classes [S5]. All sources were retrieved on the same date, so check your own university's rule. One exception is that you may apply again if you change your program or program level, for example from undergraduate to master's [S1].

You must have valid health insurance throughout your stay, so arrange private insurance if you miss GSS [S1][S2]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with SGK (hotline 170) [S5].

question: Is the Turkish student residence permit card fee 810 TL or 964 TL?
answer:
The sources disagree. METU says that for 2026 you pay only a card fee of 964.0 TL as a student residence permit applicant, and no visa or residence permit fees [S1]. Sabancı University tells you to bring more than 810₺ in cash to pay, but it gives no year for that figure and notes the fee changes every year [S5]. The METU figure is explicitly dated 2026, so 964 TL looks like the current amount. The 810₺ figure is probably an older amount.

To pay, you can enter the accrue number (tahakkuk numarası) from your online application at dijital.gib.gov.tr. Use a computer, not a phone [S1]. If you pay at a bank or tax office, get the receipt stamped and keep the original [S5].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm the current fee with the immigration authority or your university's international office.

question: Does the German student visa checklist for Indian applicants require a passport with just one blank page?
answer: No. The checklist for Indian applicants asks for a valid passport issued within the last 10 years with at least 2 empty pages, so a passport with only one blank page would not meet the listed requirement [S1]. You also need to bring copies of the passport's data page (A4, 2 copies) [S1]. This checklist was last updated in September 2024 [S2]. Other German missions set similar rules: the UK mission asks for at least 2 consecutive blank pages [S3], and the Canada mission asks for at least 2 subsequent blank pages [S4]. Please confirm the current requirements with the German Mission in India before your appointment, because the rules can change and this is not legal advice.

question: I'm 29 and studying in Germany. Roughly how much is statutory student health insurance per month?
answer: As a 29-year-old student, you qualify for the reduced statutory (public) student rate, which applies until you turn 30 [S1][S2][S5]. The sources give different amounts, though: about 120–130 euros per month [S1], around €110 per month [S2], and about 140 euros a month [S5]. One visa checklist also budgets €137 per month for insurance costs [S3]. All sources were retrieved on the same date (2026-11-18), so recency doesn't settle the difference. The DAAD web page (€120–130) and Study in Germany (€140) are probably closer to current rates than the PDF guide (€110), but the sources don't confirm this. Plan for this soon: once you reach 30, you'll have to pay the standard contribution [S1]. That costs 250 euros or more per month [S5], so private insurance may then be cheaper [S1]. Please confirm the exact current rate with a statutory insurer or your university's student services; this isn't legal advice.

question: If I want to stay and look for work after graduating, how do the options in Germany and Türkiye compare?
answer: Germany: the sources describe a specific post-study job-search permit; for Türkiye they only describe job-hunting support, not a residence option. In Germany, after earning a degree you can apply for a residence permit under § 20 Para. 1 No. 1 AufenthG for 18 months to look for a job [S4]. This is only available immediately after graduation [S4]. If you take a job abroad first, you can later request a 12-month 'Chance card' job-seeking visa, but it does not let you work without restriction [S4]. With a German degree, you can usually join the labour market directly [S3]. In Türkiye, the sources point you to campus career fairs and university career centres for job and internship opportunities [S1]. They note that a student residence permit does not include a work permit, which is issued by the General Directorate of International Labour [S5]. The sources do not say whether Türkiye offers a post-graduation job-search residence permit. This is not legal advice, so please confirm with the immigration authorities.

question: I have a student residence permit from France and want to study one semester in Germany. Do I need a German residence permit?
answer: The sources only partly answer this. If you are a non-EU (third-country) student coming from a KIT partner university in Europe on an exchange program, KIT says you must apply for a confirmation of mobility within the EU under the EU REST Directive (2016/801). [S1] The sources do not say whether this confirmation replaces a German residence permit. They also do not cover other universities or non-exchange stays. As a general rule, non-EU citizens who want to study in Germany for more than 90 days must apply for a residence permit at the local foreigners' registration office within the first three months. [S3] However, that source does not mention people who already hold a student permit from another EU country, such as France. Please ask your host university's International Office and the local foreigners' office to confirm what applies to you. This is not legal advice.

question: Do student assistant jobs at my university count toward my work-day limit in Germany?
answer: Generally no: student or research assistant jobs at a higher education institution are exempt from the work-day limit, and there is no limit on how much you can work in them [S2][S4]. However, you must still inform the immigration (foreigners') office [S2][S4]. One source puts it more strictly, saying such university employment is permitted throughout the year but requires authorization from the Foreigners' Office in your residence permit [S5]. That source also says ordinary jobs are capped at 140 full days per calendar year [S5]. Check your residence permit and ask your office which applies to you. If you are unsure whether your job counts as an on-campus job, ask student services or your Foreigners Registration Department office [S2][S3]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with your local foreigners' office before you start.

question: Does my student residence permit let me work in Germany, and is it the same in Türkiye?
answer:
For Türkiye, no: your student residence permit does not by itself let you work, and you need an official work permit [S2][S3]. You cannot apply for this permit yourself. You first need to find a job, and then the company that hires you applies for the work permit [S2]. The limits depend on your level of study:
- **Undergraduate:** only after your first year, only part-time, and only for jobs outside the university/campus [S2].
- **Graduate:** from your first year, full-time or part-time, but also only for jobs outside the university/campus [S2].

If you work without a work permit, the Migration Office could cancel your residence permit [S1].

For Germany, the sources only say that you apply for a residence permit for the purpose of studying at the foreigners' office [S4]. They do not say whether that permit lets you work, so I can't answer that part.

This is not legal advice. Please confirm with the responsible authority before taking a job.
